steps.title: A records a physical-time event
steps.narration: A reads millisecond 1000, which exceeds its prior physical component 995.
steps.outcome: A anchors the tuple to its advancing wall clock and resets the logical component.
steps.invariant: An HLC physical component never decreases.

steps.title: Clock regression increments logical time
steps.narration: A wall time regresses to 997, so a second local event retains physical 1000 and increments logical to one.
steps.outcome: The second event remains ordered after the first without moving backward in physical time.
steps.invariant: When wall time does not exceed stored physical time, a local event increments the logical component.

steps.title: A sends a stamped mutation
steps.narration: The send is an event, so A increments its logical component and attaches (1000,2).
steps.outcome: The message carries a timestamp later than both A updates.
steps.invariant: Every send advances the sender HLC before publishing its tuple.

steps.title: B merges a future remote tuple
steps.narration: B receives at physical 998 and chooses physical max 1000, then advances beyond the remote logical value to three.
steps.outcome: B is causally after A even though B wall time is behind.
steps.invariant: A receive timestamp must compare greater than the message timestamp.

steps.title: B wall clock catches up
steps.narration: At physical 1005, B records a local event and resets the logical component.
steps.outcome: Physical time resumes carrying the ordering once it exceeds the stored component.
steps.invariant: Logical time resets to zero only when the chosen physical component strictly advances.

steps.title: A merges B reply
steps.narration: B sends at (1005,1); A receives it at wall time 1002 and advances to (1005,2).
steps.outcome: The ledger has a causality-compatible order with timestamps close to wall time.
steps.invariant: HLC ties still require a deterministic node-id tie-breaker; HLC does not make physical clocks exact.

production.scenario: A cloud firewall control plane stamps every policy change with a hybrid logical clock so auditors can page through cross-region updates using one sortable cursor without trusting NTP alone.
components: Submits firewall rule changes from a regional admin session
Owns policy writes for one firewall management region
Produces causally safe timestamps that still track wall-clock time
Authoritative desired state for firewall policies
Stores every accepted policy change with its HLC stamp
Resumes change replay after a regional failover using the last seen HLC cursor
flows: An engineer pushes an urgent firewall block from the portal during an active abuse event.
Before the write commits, the config API asks the HLC service for a timestamp that respects any remote updates it has already observed.
The firewall policy store records the new desired state together with a timestamp that is both sortable and causally safe.
The committed policy update flows into the cross-region audit log with the same timestamp as the source-of-truth write.
resume scan from last HLC cursor
After failover, the rollback worker can continue replaying from the last HLC it processed without double-applying older policy changes.
reseed recovered region in HLC order
The recovered region rebuilds its local cache in the same causal order even if its wall clock lags behind another region.
